overview.text: North Korea and South Korea are the two states on the Korean Peninsula. Their separation grew from the end of Japanese colonial rule in 1945, when Soviet and American forces occupied areas north and south of the 38th parallel. Rival governments formed, and North Korean forces crossed southward in June 1950, beginning the Korean War. Fighting stopped under a July 1953 military armistice, which fixed a military demarcation line and created a demilitarized zone by pulling forces back two kilometers on each side. The armistice called for a later peaceful settlement; it did not itself reunify the peninsula. The demarcation line should not be confused with the earlier, straight 38th-parallel division.

key_facts.text: The postwar occupation division initially followed the 38th parallel.
North Korean troops attacked southward on June 25, 1950.
The armistice was signed on July 27, 1953.
Each side was to withdraw two kilometers from the military demarcation line.
The resulting demilitarized zone was intended as a buffer against renewed fighting.

overview.text: Slavery was deeply embedded in several societies of classical Greece and Rome, although its forms differed by city and period. In Athens, enslaved people could be privately owned, while Sparta relied on helots, a distinct system of unfree labor. Enslavement could follow capture in war or purchase, rather than a single modern racial classification. In Rome, some enslaved people gained freedom, becoming freedmen or freedwomen. Freedom did not erase social distinctions: surviving inscriptions identify some people as freedmen or freedwomen and connect them to former owners. Studying these different legal positions reveals why a single picture of “ancient slavery” misses important differences across the classical world.

key_facts.text: Athens and Sparta developed different institutions of unfree labor.
Spartan helots differed from enslaved people owned individually in Athens.
War captives and slave trading were routes into enslavement in Greek societies.
In Rome, a freedman was called a libertus.
Roman inscriptions may identify former enslaved people with L or LIB.

overview.text: Slavery in Brazil lasted from colonial times into the late nineteenth century and depended heavily on the forced labor of Africans and their descendants. Enslaved people resisted in many ways, including by forming quilombos, communities of mutual aid and refuge. Abolition came through years of pressure, resistance, and legislation, rather than a single act of generosity. A law in 1871 addressed children born to enslaved mothers; the Lei Áurea, or Golden Law, finally declared slavery extinct on 13 May 1888. Princess Isabel signed it as imperial regent in the name of Emperor Pedro II. Its brief text ended legal bondage but did not set out a program of support for people newly freed.

key_facts.text: Quilombos were communities associated with resistance to enslavement.
The 1871 Law of the Free Womb addressed children born to enslaved mothers.
The Golden Law is Law No. 3,353, dated 13 May 1888.
Princess Isabel sanctioned the law while acting as imperial regent.
The law’s two articles abolished slavery and revoked conflicting provisions.

overview.text: Ruhollah Khomeini was a Shiʿa cleric whose opposition to Iran’s shah made him a central figure in the 1978–79 revolution. After years of exile, including time in Iraq and then France, he returned to Tehran on 1 February 1979 as the monarchy was collapsing. His movement helped establish the Islamic Republic, with Khomeini occupying its leading religious and political office until his death in 1989. He argued for guardianship of the Islamic jurist, an idea that shaped the new constitutional order. The revolution involved many political and social groups; Khomeini’s eventual authority should not be mistaken for sole authorship of the uprising.

key_facts.text: Khomeini returned to Iran from exile on 1 February 1979.
The shah left Iran in January 1979.
The Pahlavi regime collapsed in February 1979.
The Islamic Republic’s constitution placed leadership under a religious jurist.
Khomeini died in 1989.

overview.text: Viking longships were long, narrow Scandinavian vessels especially useful for carrying crews in warfare and raids during the Viking Age. Their overlapping wooden planks formed a clinker-built hull, and a shallow draft helped them enter river mouths and approach shores. Crews could row when winds failed and set a square sail for longer passages. Surviving wrecks show variation rather than one standard design: Skuldelev 2, for example, was a large warship later reconstructed by the Viking Ship Museum at Roskilde. Longships also carried people across seas within Scandinavian networks. Wider cargo vessels were another important Viking ship type, so the longship should not stand for every Norse vessel.

key_facts.text: Clinker construction overlaps each plank with the one below it.
Oars and a square sail provided complementary propulsion.
A shallow draft aided travel into river mouths.
Skuldelev 2 was a large longship built by Scandinavians in Dublin around 1042.
The Sea Stallion from Glendalough is a reconstruction of Skuldelev 2.

references.title: The Longships of the Viking Age

overview.text: Edward I, nicknamed Longshanks, ruled England from 1272 to 1307. His reign joined legal and parliamentary activity to military expansion. In Wales he fought Llywelyn ap Gruffudd and extended English royal authority, building a network of castles to secure conquest. Edward also intervened in Scotland and defeated William Wallace’s forces at Falkirk in 1298, but Scottish resistance continued. Expensive campaigns in Wales, Scotland, and France required heavy taxation and increased the king’s need to summon Parliament. The broad assembly of 1295 is often called the Model Parliament because it included nobles, clergy, knights, and townspeople. Edward died in 1307 while heading north for another Scottish campaign.

key_facts.text: Edward I reigned from 1272 to 1307.
He was known as Longshanks.
He built stone castles at strategic sites in Wales.
His forces defeated William Wallace at Falkirk in 1298.
The 1295 Model Parliament included knights and townspeople as well as barons and clergy.

overview.text: Edward of Woodstock, later called the Black Prince, was the eldest son of England’s Edward III and heir to the throne. He fought beside his father at Crécy in 1346 during the Hundred Years’ War. A decade later he commanded the Anglo-Gascon victory at Poitiers, where French king John II was captured. Edward also governed Aquitaine, where his manner and spending provoked hostility. He became seriously ill and died in 1376, before Edward III, so he never became king. His son Richard later succeeded Edward III as Richard II. The familiar nickname “Black Prince” appears in later usage, and should not be treated as the title he used in his lifetime.

key_facts.text: Edward of Woodstock was Edward III’s eldest son.
He fought at Crécy in 1346.
He won at Poitiers in 1356, where John II of France was captured.
He died in 1376 before his father.
His son later became Richard II.

overview.text: The Bronze Age names a broad phase in which bronze metalworking became important in many societies, but it has no single worldwide start or end date. Bronze is usually an alloy of copper and tin; obtaining these materials could link distant regions through trade. In Scandinavia, for example, bronze technology developed despite a lack of local copper and tin, encouraging contact with central and southern Europe. In parts of West Asia, Bronze Age cities also used writing: merchants at Kanesh recorded transactions on cuneiform tablets. The period’s technologies and social changes varied widely, and iron did not replace bronze everywhere at once. Historians therefore use regional chronologies rather than one universal Bronze Age calendar.

key_facts.text: Bronze is an alloy chiefly of copper and tin.
Metropolitan Museum timelines give different Bronze Age date ranges for northern and eastern Europe.
Scandinavian bronze production depended on imported copper and tin.
Old Assyrian merchants at Kanesh wrote trade records in cuneiform.
A Kanesh tablet described by the Met dates to the twentieth–nineteenth centuries BCE.

overview.text: Italian unification, or the Risorgimento, was a nineteenth-century movement that brought many states of the Italian peninsula into a new kingdom. Piedmont-Sardinia provided the monarchy and much of the diplomatic leadership, while Giuseppe Garibaldi’s 1860 campaign toppled the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in the south. Plebiscites also brought northern territories into the growing state. The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed on 17 March 1861 under Victor Emmanuel II. Unification was not geographically complete that day: Venetia joined in 1866 and Rome was taken in 1870, later becoming the capital. The process combined war, diplomacy, popular politics, and conquest, with different outcomes for people across the peninsula.

key_facts.text: Garibaldi campaigned against the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in 1860.
The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed on 17 March 1861.
The royal dynasty came from Piedmont-Sardinia.
Venetia joined the kingdom in 1866.
Italian forces entered Rome in 1870.

overview.text: The Zimmermann Telegram was a coded message sent in January 1917 by German foreign secretary Arthur Zimmermann to Germany’s representative in Mexico. It proposed a German-Mexican alliance if the United States entered World War I against Germany, offering financial help and support for Mexican recovery of Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. British codebreakers intercepted and deciphered the message. When its contents became public, it intensified American anger toward Germany; Germany’s renewed unrestricted submarine warfare was another major factor in the decision for war. The United States declared war in April 1917. The proposal was conditional, and Mexico did not enter the war on Germany’s side.

key_facts.text: Arthur Zimmermann was Germany’s foreign secretary.
The message proposed an alliance with Mexico if the United States entered the war.
It named Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona as territory Germany would support Mexico in recovering.
British Room 40 codebreakers intercepted the cable.
Its disclosure helped shift U.S. opinion before the April 1917 declaration of war.
